title: Pauri 30, meaning: He sees, unseen
hookLine: the old picture of three powers that make, keep and end the world; all act by His order, and He sees them though they do not see Him (Japji 30)

lines: A KID ON THE CLIMBING FRAME.
cards: A small kid on a climbing frame, deep in some game only they understand. On a bench at the edge of the playground, a parent is watching. The kid never looks over.
Doesn't need to. They climb higher and braver, because someone has an eye on them. Put a stranger on that same bench, and the same watching means something else.
Being seen can be a threat or a blessing. It depends on who's looking, and how. Pauri 30 ends with someone who sees and is not seen.

teach.b: The stanza names the three disciples. Ik sansaaree: one who brings forth the world. Ik bhanddaaree: one who keeps the stores, who sustains.
Ik laae deebaan: one who holds court, who judges and brings things to an end.

Commentators connect these three with a picture from Hindu tradition that Guru Nanak's hearers knew well: Brahma who creates, Vishnu who preserves, and Shiva who ends and transforms. Nanak doesn't argue with the picture.
He places it. Next line: jiv tis bhaavai tivai chalaavai, jiv hovai furmaan.

As it pleases Him, so He makes them move, as His order is. Furmaan: a command, the word for a royal decree. Even the greatest powers people could imagine work within the one order, the hukam from Pauri 1.
Then the turn, the heart of the stanza: oh vekhai onaa nadar na aavai.

teach.h: HE SEES THEM; THEY DON'T SEE HIM.
teach.b: He sees them, but He does not come into their sight. And Nanak adds: bahutaa eh viddaan.
This is the great wonder. Not a warning. A wonder.
Sikh teachers hear this seeing as care, the way the Granth elsewhere speaks of the Creator making and then watching over what was made.
The One who can't be seen is not a stranger on the bench. More like the parent: the eye that lets you play.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 30 is commonly explained as placing every power, however great, within the one divine order, and its closing line, He sees them though they do not see Him, is often read as a picture of the Creator's care.

o: a warning to behave, since God watches

games.q: what's inside Pauri 30 — tap the pairs.
p: one who brings forth the world
one who holds court and ends

s: Pauri 30 mocks the picture of three powers
Nanak doesn't argue with the picture; he places it within the one order.
in Pauri 30, the three powers cannot see the One who sees them
oh vekhai onaa nadar na aavai.
Nanak ends the stanza by calling this a warning
he calls it bahutaa viddaan: the great wonder.

games.q: three great powers make, keep and end the world. in Pauri 30, what do they move by?
o: the One's order, as it pleases Him.
games.why: jiv tis bhaavai tivai chalaavai, jiv hovai furmaan: as it pleases Him, as His order is. and He sees them, though they don't see Him.

practice: Remember a time you felt seen kindly: a teacher who noticed you, a friend who knew what was wrong before you said it, a grandparent watching you with pride.
Sit inside that memory as if that kind attention were still on you, here, right now; you don't need to look back at it. Breathe, and let yourself be seen.

wordCard.voice: Viddaan, wonder. Three powers that make, keep and end the world, all moving by one order; and the One sees them, though they cannot see Him. This is the great wonder.

orig.s: ਓਹੁ ਵੇਖੈ ਓਨਾ ਨਦਰਿ ਨ ਆਵੈ

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 30: He sees them, but does not come into their sight.

carryVoice: Your line: seen, though unseen. Even the greatest powers move inside one order. That's day two hundred fourteen.
